appraisal_events.evidence: Combray gossip pities him as « aveuglé par la tendresse », Percepied makes the whole company « rire aux larmes » with his joke about the music made « dans c'te boîte-là », and the narrator confirms the fall: « il se voyait avec sa fille dans le dernier bas-fond », his new « humilité, ce respect pour ceux qui se trouvaient au-dessus de lui », « une résultante presque mécanique de toutes les déchéances », a man « en train de mourir de chagrin ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage's dominant movement is M. Vinteuil's social and personal collapse: the village first scandalizes and then openly ridicules his household, and the narrator ratifies the fall as real by showing Vinteuil internalizing Combray's most hostile verdict on himself and adopting the deferential manners of the déclassé. The narrator withholds moral condemnation and treats his grief with compassion, but does not soften the social descent itself.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Quel homme exquis, nous dit-il [...] avec la même enthousiaste vénération qui tient de spirituelles et jolies bourgeoises en respect et sous le charme d'une duchesse, fût-elle laide et sotte » ; Vinteuil finds Swann's amiability « un appui si honorable et si délicieux » that he dares not use the invitation — while the narrator glosses Swann's approach as « cette orgueilleuse charité de l'homme du monde » whose gestures « chatouillent [...] l'amour-propre de celui qui les donne », and closes on Swann regretting the lapsed invitation only because he wanted information about a namesake.
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann is locally raised by Vinteuil's open veneration and by the deference of a man too grateful to accept his invitation, an asymmetry the duchess simile makes explicit. The narrator simultaneously ironizes that elevation, exposing the condescension and self-love inside Swann's charity and puncturing it with the petty motive revealed at the end.

status_effects.explanation: He falls to the bottom of Combray's esteem — an object of gossip and of Percepied's public joke — and behaves accordingly, deferring to people who were formerly beneath him.

He is shown avoiding acquaintances, aging in months, spending whole days at his wife's grave, and dying of grief; he has no leverage over anyone and is entirely at the mercy of his daughter's conduct and of public talk.
Vinteuil's enthusiastic veneration and awed refusal of the invitation position Swann far above him, on the footing the narrator's duchess comparison assigns him.

The narrator's framing of his kindness as proud, self-flattering charity, and the closing disclosure that he regretted the lapsed visit for a private errand, lower how the passage asks us to judge him even as his standing rises.

ambiguities: The narrator relays Combray's scandalized talk and Percepied's mockery without endorsing their moral verdict — indeed he defends Vinteuil's suffering and his undiminished cult for his daughter — yet he confirms the social descent as fact; the diminishment should be read as social and emotional rather than as narrator-endorsed moral blame.

Swann's local movement is genuinely double-edged: Vinteuil's veneration plainly elevates him, while the narrator's irony about his « orgueilleuse charité » and the closing revelation of his self-interested motive cut against it, so the net direction depends on whether the reported admiration or the narratorial framing is weighted.
